Decoupled head In object detection, the conflict between
classification and regression tasks is a well-known prob-
lem [27, 34]. Thus the decoupled head for classification
and localization is widely used in the most of one-stage and
two-stage detectors [16, 29, 35, 34]. However, as YOLO
series' backbones and feature pyramids ( e.g., FPN [13],
PAN [20].) continuously evolving, their detection heads re-
main coupled as shown in Fig. 2.
Our two analytical experiments indicate that the coupled
detection head may harm the performance. 1). Replacing
YOLO's head with a decoupled one greatly improves the
converging speed as shown in Fig. 3. 2). The decoupled
head is essential to the end-to-end version of YOLO

Strong data augmentation We add Mosaic and MixUp
into our augmentation strategies to boost YOLOX's per-
formance. Mosaic is an efficient augmentation strategy
proposed by ultralytics-YOLOv3 2. It is then widely used
in YOLOv4 [1], YOLOv5 [7] and other detectors [3].
MixUp [10] is originally designed for image classification
task but then modified in BoF [38] for object detection train-
ing. We adopt the MixUp and Mosaic implementation in
our model and close it for the last 15 epochs, achieving
42.0% AP in Tab. 2. After using strong data augmentation,

augmentation In our experiments,
all the models keep almost the same learning schedule and
optimizing parameters as depicted in 2.1. However, we
found that the suitable augmentation strategy varies across
different size of models. As Tab. 5 shows, while apply-
ing MixUp for YOLOX-L can improve AP by 0.9%, it is
better to weaken the augmentation for small models like
YOLOX-Nano. Specifically, we remove the mix up aug-
mentation and weaken the mosaic (reduce the scale range
from [0.1, 2.0] to [0.5, 1.5]) when training small models,
i.e., YOLOX-S, YOLOX-Tiny, and YOLOX-Nano. Such a
modification improves YOLOX-Nano's AP from 24.0% to
25.3%.
For large models, we also found that stronger augmenta-
tion is more helpful. Indeed, our MixUp implementation is
part of heavier than the original version in [38]. Inspired
by Copypaste [6], we jittered both images by a random sam-
pled scale factor

There is a tradition to show the SOTA comparing table as
in Tab. 6. However, keep in mind that the inference speed
of the models in this table is often uncontrolled, as speed
varies with software and hardware. We thus use the same
hardware and code base for all the YOLO series in Fig. 1,
plotting the somewhat controlled speed/accuracy curve.
We notice that there are some high performance YOLO
series with larger model sizes like Scale-YOLOv4 [30] and
YOLOv5-P6 [7]. And the current Transformer based detec-
tors [21] push the accuracy-SOTA to ∼60 AP. Due to the
time and resource limitation, we did not explore those im-
portant features in this report. However, they are already in
our scope.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Headline performance and speed-accuracy trade-offs are verified on the standard MS COCO 2017 test-dev benchmark and corroborated by winning 1st place in the CVPR 2021 Streaming Perception Challenge.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Standard COCO average precision (AP) metrics computed on held-out COCO validation and test-dev splits.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Supervised training losses (BCE classification and objectness losses, IoU regression loss) with dynamic sample assignment via SimOTA on COCO train2017.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: Reported performance metrics (e.g., 47.3% AP for YOLOX-DarkNet53, 50.0% AP for YOLOX-L, and comparisons on tiny/nano models) directly substantiate claims of exceeding prior YOLO baselines while maintaining real-time efficiency.
primary.evaluation_assessment: Empirical evaluations are conducted rigorously on the standard MS COCO benchmark (val and test-dev splits). The authors provide systematic component-by-component ablations, speed-latency-accuracy Pareto curves under consistent GPU hardware, and side-by-side comparisons with contemporary detectors (YOLOv3, YOLOv4, YOLOv5, and EfficientDet).

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Headline performance and speed-accuracy trade-offs are verified on the standard MS COCO 2017 test-dev benchmark and corroborated by winning 1st place in the CVPR 2021 Streaming Perception Challenge.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Standard COCO average precision (AP) metrics computed on held-out COCO validation and test-dev splits.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Supervised training losses (BCE classification loss, BCE objectness loss, and IoU bounding box regression loss) with dynamic sample assignment via SimOTA on COCO train2017.

primary.limitations: The authors explicitly note that higher-capacity Transformer-based detectors and extremely large models (such as YOLOv5-P6) were not explored due to computational constraints, and that the optional end-to-end NMS-free modification incurs a mild drop in AP and latency.
primary.method_assessment: The methodology is thoroughly detailed, describing architectural adjustments (decoupling classification and regression heads), the anchor-free formulation, data augmentation protocols (MixUp and Mosaic adjustments), and the dynamic top-k approximation of optimal transport (SimOTA). Training parameters, loss formulations, and ablation steps are explicitly reported.
primary.quality_rationale: The work provides clear, scoped empirical advances with transparent ablation studies, consistent hardware benchmarking, and well-supported claims on a standard computer vision benchmark.
primary.scoped_contribution: The paper introduces YOLOX, adapting the YOLO detection family to an anchor-free architecture integrated with a decoupled detection head, multi-positive center sampling, and the SimOTA dynamic label assignment strategy across multiple model scales.

scholarly_quality.rationale: The work provides clear, scoped empirical advances with transparent ablation studies, consistent hardware benchmarking, and well-supported claims on a standard computer vision benchmark.
